newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia launches fight against Moslem social ills.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia launches fight against Moslem social ills.

text.p: Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad on Wednesday declared war on social problems affecting Moslems, who make up a little over half the Malaysian population.

"We talked about social problems affecting the Moslem population in general," Mahathir told reporters after chairing a forum involving 1,000 religious leaders, Moslem cabinet ministers and state chief ministers.
Over the past few months, multicultural Malaysia has been engaged in a fresh morality drive among its 21 million people.
It is cracking down on video arcades, ordering nightclubs and karaoke lounges to close earlier and warning about the dangers of "punk" culture among youth.
The crusade has coincided with an operation against illegal immigrants, who have been blamed for a host of ills, including crime and the spreading of infectious diseases.
The vast majority of the immigrants are from Indonesia, which has lately witnessed an upsurge in Moslem unrest.
On Friday, Mahathir said the Moslem leadership planned "to launch a campaign to fight against the spread of social ills".

The Moslem leadership is concerned about the involvement of Malays, who are all Moslem, in social problems such as incest and drug-taking. Most of the 200,000 heroin addicts are Malays, the Home Ministry has said.

"We acknowledge in almost all the social problems in the country, Malays form the majority. This is very embarrassing," said Abdul Hamid Othman, minister in the Prime Minister's Department, in an interview published in the Star newspaper on Wednesday.
Abdul Hamid said a recent study on incest showed Moslems constituted 90 percent of the reported cases.
Although often an acerbic critic of the West and its ways, Mahathir told the forum that foreign influences could not be shut out of the country, adding: "We do not blame others."
Mahathir did not mention the unrest among Indonesian Moslems in his hour-long speech to the conference. It was not clear if it was discussed in closed-door discussions afterward.

Last Thursday, rioters set fire to a church and a Chinese Buddhist temple, wrecked four other churches and looted shops in a town in Indonesia's West Java. It was the latest in a string of such attacks that appeared aimed at the small, but economically dominant, Chinese minority.
Malaysia this week closed its border with Indonesia's Borneo province of West Kalimantan after clashes between Dayak tribespeople and Moslem settlers.
